list.row: 23 documents, 29 quotations verified | §6 [M13], [M14]
list.sentence: Ambassador at Large Jessup's review proposed that "A considerably expanded information program both in Communist and non-Communist areas of Asia is called for", to align the United States with Asian nationalism ( , the National Security Council's report on the program conceded that "the trend toward accommodation to Communist pressures in the area continued" ( , Ambassador Reischauer in judged that Embassy and information-service work in Japan had "met with some success" intellectually while "the basic emotional response remains unchanged" ( , and the Information Agency's area office reported in that the American image in Asia "depended more on the state of bi-lateral relations … than on developments within the US" ( , Twenty-three documents carry the argument below.

list.sentence: Third, the full round of embassy reports on information-program effectiveness: a search for the Department's circular asking every major post to assess its program found one printed reply, from Saigon; the rest sit in the State Department's decimal file under class 511 (the class the filing manual labels "International Informational and Educational Relations, Cultural Affairs and Programs"). **Scope.** I read the 72 postwar volumes on East Asia, Southeast Asia, China, Japan, Korea and Indochina from to , plus nine volumes on the information program and public diplomacy, in which a document counted only if it named an Asian place: 81 volumes and about 35,000 documents, with front matter and editorial notes excluded.

list.sentence: I did not count every use of "face". **Which end date.** I stopped at because the volumes were outside this pass; including them would add the Reagan-era public diplomacy program. ## Findings From the start, officials judged the program by whether it could put the United States on the side of Asian nationalism — and doubted it could In Jessup's review of Far Eastern policy proposed an information program "to demonstrate our understanding and sympathy for the nationalist aspirations of the Asian peoples and to expose the menace to these aspirations created by Soviet imperialism" ( , The Psychological Strategy Board's Thailand plan added that "Southeast Asia is not a political entity but that each nation is an entity basically different from the others and requires special treatment" ( , When the posts were asked in how effective their work was, Saigon measured reach — films, libraries, English classes oversubscribed — and read it as "intense interest in US by educated groups", while admitting that Viet Minh broadcasts "go unanswered" in the countryside ( , The annual reports to the National Security Council were candid: in the agency had to answer "mixed emotions regarding the use of atomic weapons against Asiatic peoples" and propaganda "designed to stir up race hatred" ( , and by "Despite all efforts, the trend toward accommodation to Communist pressures in the area continued" ( , A belief about "the Oriental mind" shaped the advice: aid looked like weakness, and only American staying power would persuade Fourteen documents in the scope use the phrase "Oriental mind" — more than half of the 25 in the whole series, although these volumes hold only about one document in nine — so it was a habit of thinking about this region rather than a commonplace of the series.
